# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Everyday decisions are often made during physical effort, but it is unclear how physical effort changes decision-making in older adults. Effort could reduce the quality of the evidence people accumulate, change how much evidence they require before responding, or bias them toward one response. We tested these possibilities in `r v("n_final")` older adults who judged whether two tones or two visual patterns were the same or different while holding a handgrip at low (5%) or high (40%) force, with pupil size recorded throughout. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model separated the components of each decision. High effort did not reduce the quality of the evidence, and its effects did not depend on how difficult the discrimination was. Instead, high effort shifted evidence accumulation toward "same" responses on every trial, which lowered accuracy on the most difficult trials with a different probe. Effort did not meaningfully change how much evidence participants required, and it did not change their starting bias. `r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: two sentences on what the pupil showed.]")` Physical effort therefore changed how older adults mapped evidence onto responses, not how well they took in that evidence.

# 1 Introduction {.unnumbered}

Many everyday decisions are made while the body is working: judging a gap in traffic while gripping a steering wheel, or reading a label while carrying groceries. Laboratory work shows that combining a cognitive task with a motor task costs older adults more than younger adults [@verhaeghen2003]. Sustained isometric force is one such motor demand. Effortful handgrip impairs cognitive control [@azer2021detrimental] and working memory [@azer2023] in older adults. Chapter 1 tested younger adults with the same handgrip manipulation. Harder trials were less accurate and slower in every task, high effort slowed responses in the visual discrimination task only, and task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure, suggesting that the two drew on separate resources at these effort levels. Pupil size across the trial was larger under high effort in every task, whereas task difficulty affected only an exploratory measure of the response to the probe. The present chapter asks how the same manipulation changes decision-making in older adults, using a model that separates the processes that accuracy and response time (RT) combine. In this chapter, effort refers to physical effort throughout.

Accuracy and RT alone cannot say why performance changes under effort. Lower accuracy could mean that the stimulus was encoded less well, or that participants answered on less evidence. The drift-diffusion model separates these possibilities [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. It treats a two-choice decision as noisy evidence accumulating until it reaches one of two boundaries. Drift rate (*v*) is the average direction and speed of accumulation, boundary separation (*a*) is how much evidence is required before responding, the starting point (*z*) is a bias toward one response before the stimulus appears, and non-decision time (*t*~0~) covers encoding and response execution.

In older adults, the most consistent age differences are wider boundaries and longer non-decision times, whereas drift is often similar to that of younger adults on simple perceptual tasks [@ratcliff2001aging; @theisen2021age]. Older adults also set boundaries more conservatively than would maximize their reward rate [@starns2010effects]. The model therefore separates a loss of evidence quality from a change in response caution, which in the diffusion model is boundary separation. Both have been proposed as effects of physical effort.

The first account treats effort as a competitor for limited processing capacity [@kahneman1973attention; @wickens2008]. If holding a 40% grip uses capacity needed to compare the probe with the standard, evidence about the stimulus should become less informative. In a same–different task coded by response, this predicts a smaller difference between drift on trials with a different probe and drift on trials with an identical probe. Such a reduction in evidence quality differs from a uniform shift of drift toward one response on all trials. That second pattern is a change in the drift criterion: the reference against which evidence counts as favoring "same" or "different" [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. A uniform shift can lower accuracy on difficult different trials without any loss of evidence quality, so the two must be estimated separately. Because a shared capacity limit should cost most where discrimination is hardest [@kahneman1973attention], this account also predicts that any loss of evidence quality is largest on the hardest trials, so that effort and task difficulty interact.

The second account treats effort as a change in how participants set their decision policy, not in the evidence itself. Under high effort, participants could require more evidence before responding, to protect accuracy, or less evidence, to end each effortful trial sooner. The first possibility predicts wider boundaries under high effort and the second narrower ones, so the direction of the effort effect on boundary separation distinguishes them. Effort could also bias responding. A bias set before the stimulus appears would move the starting point, whereas a bias in how evidence is evaluated would shift the drift criterion. Neither predicts a loss of evidence quality.

Pupil size provides a trial-by-trial measure that increases with processing load [@beatty1982; @vanderwel2018pupil] and with physical exertion [@zenon2014pupil]. Older adults have smaller pupils and a narrower range of dilation than younger adults [@winn1994factors; @piquado2010pupillometry]. In diffusion-model analyses, trial-wise pupil responses have been related to specific parameters. In a reinforcement-learning task, larger dilation on choices between similarly valued options predicted higher decision thresholds [@cavanagh2014], and across several decision tasks, larger pupil responses predicted smaller choice biases [@degee2020pupil]. Pupil responses, however, also scale with decision uncertainty and response time [@urai2017]. A pupil–boundary association could therefore arise because longer decisions produce larger pupil responses, not because the pupil response came before the boundary was set. Testing the direction of the relation requires pupil measures taken before the decision, as well as measures that end before the response.

We combined both approaches in older adults performing auditory and visual same–different tasks under low (5%) and high (40%) handgrip effort. The first analysis was a diffusion model of choices and RTs. It tested whether high effort reduced evidence quality (the capacity account), shifted the drift criterion, or changed boundary separation or starting point (the state accounts). The second analysis added trial-wise pupil measures to the same model. It tested whether pupil size tracked the effort effect, which decision parameter tracked the task-evoked pupil response, and whether pupil measures taken before the decision predicted boundary separation.

# 2 Methods {.unnumbered}

## 2.1 Participants {.unnumbered}

Community-dwelling adults aged 60–90 years were recruited around the University of California, Riverside. All were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, and had no contraindication for MRI, no current psychotropic medication, no neurological disorder and no major systemic condition (including diabetes). Of `r v("n_enrolled")` enrolled participants, `r nw(v("n_excluded"))` were excluded (suspected mild cognitive impairment; possible essential tremor). That left `r v("n_final")` older adults (@tbl-demographics). Under the inclusion criteria, `r v("n_adt") + v("n_vdt") - v("n_final")` participants contributed data to both tasks and `r nw(2 * v("n_final") - v("n_adt") - v("n_vdt"))` to only one (auditory, `r v("n_adt")`; visual, `r v("n_vdt")`). Participants gave written informed consent and received course credit or payment. Procedures were approved by the University of California, Riverside Institutional Review Board.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Participant characteristics"
ch3_tbl_demographics(tbl$T1_demographics)
```

## 2.2 Task and stimuli {.unnumbered}

Participants performed an auditory discrimination task (ADT) and a visual discrimination task (VDT) in the MRI scanner while squeezing a dynamometer with the left hand (@fig-design). After a blank gray screen (1.5–4.5 s), a grip gauge appeared for 3 s with a target at 5% (low effort) or 40% (high effort) of the participant's maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). Participants held the grip until the probe ended. After a 0.25-s blank and a 0.5-s fixation dot, a standard and a probe stimulus (0.1 s each) were presented 0.5 s apart. In the ADT, the standard was a 1000-Hz tone, and the probe was identical or 8, 16, 32 or 64 Hz higher. In the VDT, the standard was a Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, 4°), and the probe was identical or had a contrast 0.06, 0.12, 0.24 or 0.48 higher. The two smaller offsets were grouped as Hard, the two larger as Easy, and identical probes as Standard.

In this response-signal procedure, participants withheld their response until a cue appeared 0.25 s after probe offset. They then had 3 s to answer "different" (right index finger) or "same" (right middle finger), followed by a confidence rating that is not analyzed here. Each task had five blocks of 30 trials. Each block crossed the five probe levels with the two effort levels, three times each, in pseudorandom order. Effort was therefore known before each trial, but the stimulus type was known only at probe onset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_design()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F1_design_model.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

## 2.3 Sessions and maximum voluntary contraction {.unnumbered}

The tasks were completed across three sessions on separate days. In Session 1, participants watched instructional videos and practiced at least 60 trials of each task without the grip, and their MVC was measured. They then practiced both tasks with the grip and confidence ratings until the experimenter judged that they understood them. In Sessions 2 and 3, participants performed one task each in the scanner (order counterbalanced), each preceded by a short practice block. MVC was the mean force across three maximal 5-s squeezes, with about 30 s of rest between them. It was measured again in the scanner in Session 2, and that value set the 5% and 40% targets in Sessions 2 and 3.

## 2.4 Apparatus {.unnumbered}

The task ran in Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997psychophysics; @kleiner2007s] in MATLAB R2022b. Visual stimuli were projected with a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies; 480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) and viewed through a head-coil mirror (effective viewing distance 12 cm). Sounds were delivered through MRI-compatible earbuds (Newmatic Medical; 30 dB noise reduction). Responses were recorded with a RESPONSEpixx button box, grip force with an MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs; 100 Hz) and pupil diameter with a TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies; 2000 Hz). The background was mid-gray. The gauge's force bar covered less than 1% of the screen, so it changed mean luminance by less than 1% between effort levels, in the direction that would constrict the pupil under high effort.

## 2.5 Behavioral data processing {.unnumbered}

RT was recorded from the response cue. For modeling it was measured from probe onset, by adding the fixed 0.35-s interval between probe onset and the cue, so that the decision clock starts when evidence becomes available and the non-decision time absorbs the enforced delay. Of `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_raw"))` recorded trials, `r nw(v("n_trials_negative_rt"))` with a negative RT were removed. A further `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_cutoff_excluded"))` with a cue-locked RT below 0.20 s were removed as anticipatory. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_primary"))` trials (Table S1). Cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s were used in sensitivity analyses. Overall accuracy was at or below .55 for `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants. They were retained in the primary analysis and excluded in a sensitivity analysis.

## 2.6 Pupillometry {.unnumbered}

Blinks and other artifacts were removed with the ET-remove-artifacts toolbox [@mather2020isometric] and checked visually. The signal was downsampled to 250 Hz, and each sample was placed on a time axis at 4-ms steps from 3 s before squeeze onset. This axis spans the recorded epoch, which ends with the confidence window 10.7 s after squeeze onset.

The task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) was the mean pupil size 0.3–3.3 s after probe onset (4.65–7.65 s after squeeze onset) minus the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before the probe (3.85–4.35 s, the interstimulus interval). As in Chapter 1, this baseline separates the response to the probe from the slower dilation that builds up during the grip. The window starts 0.3 s after the probe to allow for pupil latency [@mathot2018] and covers the typical peak, 1–2 s after the stimulus [@dasilvacastanheira2021task]. Because the window extends past the response on most trials, the TEPR includes post-decision processing; Section 2.8 describes how this was tested. Two further measures were the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before squeeze onset (pre-squeeze baseline) and the mean pupil size during the grip (`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_start"), 2)`–`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_end"), 2)` s), relative to the pre-squeeze baseline.

Trials entered the pupil analyses if at least 50% of samples were valid in both the pre-probe baseline and the TEPR window. Each participant × task cell needed at least 20 such trials. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_pupil_final_trials"))` trials from `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` participants (Figure S1), a subset of the behavioral sample selected on recording quality. Each pupil predictor was centered within participant × task × effort and divided by the participant's pooled within-cell SD. Its slope therefore reflects trial-to-trial fluctuation around the condition mean.

## 2.7 Drift-diffusion model {.unnumbered}

### 2.7.1 Response coding {.unnumbered}

Choices and probe-locked RTs were modeled with a Wiener diffusion model [@ratcliff2008diffusion], with "different" as the upper boundary and "same" as the lower boundary. Positive drift therefore moves toward "different." The starting point measures a bias toward one response. On Standard trials, drift is negative when evidence accumulates toward the correct "same" response.

### 2.7.2 Model specification {.unnumbered}

Models were fit jointly to both tasks in brms [@burkner2017brms] with CmdStan [@cmdstan2024], using an identity link for drift, log links for boundary separation (*a*) and non-decision time (*t*~0~), and a logit link for the starting point (*z*). In the primary model (M4), drift depended on stimulus type (Standard, Hard, Easy), task, their interaction, effort and an effort × stimulus term. Boundary separation depended on stimulus type, task and effort, and the starting point on task and effort. Non-decision time had an intercept only. Participants had random intercepts on drift, boundary separation and starting point.

The effort main effect on drift shifts drift equally on all trials, toward "different" if positive and toward "same" if negative. This is a change in the drift criterion [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The effort × stimulus term (stimulus coded +1 for Hard and Easy, −1 for Standard) changes how far drift on different-stimulus trials lies from drift on Standard trials, which is a change in evidence quality.

The starting point did not depend on stimulus type, which could not be known before the trial. The boundary terms for stimulus type absorb RT differences between stimulus types. Because stimulus types were intermixed, those terms are not interpreted as strategic settings (Section 4.4). Non-decision time had no predictors because, in a response-signal design, it mainly absorbs the delay before the cue.

M4 was compared with nested models that differed in how effort, stimulus type and task entered drift and boundary separation (formulas in S6). Two variants of M4 were also fit: M4b added effort × task interactions on drift, and M4r added by-participant random effort slopes on drift and boundary separation.

### 2.7.3 Priors and estimation {.unnumbered}

Priors were weakly informative on the link scale (@supptbl-priors). The boundary-separation intercept was bounded between 0.3 and 5. Non-decision time was bounded between 0.02 s and 0.01 s below the shortest RT. Models used `r v("n_chains")` chains of `r fmt_int(v("n_iter"))` iterations, the first `r fmt_int(v("n_warmup"))` of them warmup (adapt_delta = `r fmt_num(v("adapt_delta"), 2)`, maximum tree depth `r v("max_treedepth")`). `r v("refit_models")` did not meet the convergence criterion at this length and were refit with `r fmt_int(v("n_iter_refit"))` iterations. A model was accepted if every parameter had R̂ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 400 and no divergent transitions [@vehtari2021rank]. Table S4 gives the diagnostics for every model.

## 2.8 Pupil-linked models {.unnumbered}

Each pupil-linked model added one pupil predictor to M4. Each was compared with an M4 baseline fit to the same trials. The TEPR was entered on the starting point (P1), on drift with a TEPR × stimulus term (P2) or on boundary separation (P3). The pre-squeeze baseline was entered on the starting point (P4) and on boundary separation (P5). Because the TEPR window overlapped the response, three further tests asked whether a TEPR–boundary association could reflect decision duration rather than a pupil change before the decision. First, P3 was refit after removing the slowest 20% of trials in each participant × task cell (P3 without the slowest trials). Second, boundary separation was predicted from pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response, a window that ends before the response (P7). Third, boundary separation was predicted from measures that precede the decision: the previous trial's TEPR within a block (P6) and the grip-period pupil size (P8).

Effort effects on pupil size were tested with paired *t* tests on participant means within each task. Only participants with valid trials at both effort levels were included.

## 2.9 Statistical inference {.unnumbered}

Effects are reported as posterior medians with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) and the posterior probability that the effect has the sign of its median. Whether an effect was negligible was judged against a region of practical equivalence [ROPE, @kruschke2018rejecting]. The ROPE was ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_a"), 2)` for log boundary separation and logit starting point, which corresponds to about a 5% change in *a* and about 1 percentage point in *z* near its observed value. For drift it was ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_v"), 2)`, about 1% of the drift difference between Standard and Easy trials. The proportion of the posterior inside the ROPE is reported where it bears on whether an effect is negligible.

Models were compared with Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [PSIS-LOO, @vehtari2017practical]. Observations with Pareto *k* > 0.7 were handled with moment matching and exact refits. Differences in expected log predictive density (ΔELPD) are reported with their SE, and differences smaller than about twice their SE were treated as uncertain.

Observed accuracy was analyzed with a binomial generalized linear mixed model (stimulus type × effort, plus task) in lme4 [@bates2015lme4]. Because models with random effort slopes were singular, the model used a random intercept for participant [@barr2013maximal; @bates2015parsimonious; @brauer2018lmm]. High − Low contrasts at each stimulus type were computed with emmeans [@lenth2024emmeans]. Model adequacy was checked with posterior predictive simulations of choice proportions and RT quantiles in each of the 12 task × stimulus × effort cells.

# 3 Results {.unnumbered}

## 3.1 Primary diffusion model {.unnumbered}

Allowing drift rate to differ between tasks improved out-of-sample prediction (M4 vs. M3: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", flip = TRUE)`), whereas allowing the effort effects to differ between tasks did not (M4b vs. M4: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4")`; @supptbl-model-comparison). Allowing the effort effects on drift and boundary separation to vary with difficulty did not improve prediction either (M2 vs. M1: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1", "se_delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1")`).

**Stimulus and task effects.** Drift was negative on Standard trials and positive on Easy trials (@fig-condition-params). Drift on Hard trials was also negative (low effort; ADT: `r cell_s("v_cell_ADT_Hard")`; VDT: `r cell_s("v_cell_VDT_Hard")`). Relative to Standard trials, drift was higher on Hard (`r eff("diff_hard_v")`) and Easy trials (`r eff("diff_easy_v")`), and both differences were larger in the VDT than in the ADT (Hard × VDT: `r eff("task_hard_x_vdt")`; Easy × VDT: `r eff("task_easy_x_vdt")`). Boundary separation was narrower on Hard (`r eff("diff_hard_bs", pct = TRUE)`) and Easy trials (`r eff("diff_easy_bs", pct = TRUE)`) than on Standard trials, and it did not differ between tasks (`r eff("task_bs", rope = TRUE)`). In both tasks the starting point lay above 0.5, toward the "different" boundary (ADT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_ADT")`; VDT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_VDT")`), and it was slightly lower in the VDT (`r eff("task_bias")`).


```{r}
#| label: fig-condition-params
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_condition_params()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F2_condition_parameters.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

**Effort effects.** High effort shifted drift toward "same" on all trials (drift criterion: `r eff("crit")`; @fig-effort-forest; @tbl-effort-effects). The effort × stimulus term, which indexes evidence quality, was close to zero (`r eff("qual")`). Drift decreased on trials with a different comparison stimulus (`r eff("drift_diff_trials")`); on Standard trials the change was smaller, and its interval included zero (`r eff("drift_same_trials")`). High effort widened the boundary by `r pct_s("bs")`, with the whole posterior inside the ROPE (`r fmt_rope("bs")`). The starting point did not change (`r eff("bias", rope = TRUE)`).

Under high effort, observed accuracy was lower on Hard trials (High − Low: `r acc_s("acc_high_low_Hard")`). It was slightly, but not significantly, higher on Standard trials (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Standard")`) and unchanged on Easy trials (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Easy")`; @supptbl-acc-contrasts).

## 3.2 Robustness of the effort effects {.unnumbered}

The drift criterion shift was unchanged when the effort effects were allowed to vary across participants (M4r: `r eff("crit_M4r")`). The between-participant SD of that effect was small (`r est_s("sd_effort_M4r")`). The shift was also stable at RT cutoffs of 0.15 s (`r eff("crit_thr015")`) and 0.25 s (`r eff("crit_thr025")`). Excluding the `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants with near-chance accuracy left the point estimate unchanged. With N = `r v("n_subchance_remaining")`, however, the interval included zero (`r eff("crit_subchance")`). When effort effects were allowed to differ by task (M4b), the criterion shift was larger in the ADT (`r eff("crit_ADT_M4b")`) than in the VDT (`r eff("crit_VDT_M4b")`), but the task difference was uncertain (`r eff("m4b_effort_x_task")`). The evidence-quality term was close to zero in every variant. The boundary effect was positive at the 0.25-s cutoff (`r eff("bs_thr025", pct = TRUE)`) and after the near-chance exclusion (`r eff("bs_subchance", pct = TRUE)`), but at the 0.15-s cutoff its interval included zero (`r eff("bs_thr015", pct = TRUE)`; @supptbl-robustness).

## 3.4 Model adequacy {.unnumbered}

M4 reproduced the observed choice proportions in `r v("ppc_choice_inside_M4")` of 12 condition cells (@supptbl-ppc-choice). Of the observed RT quantiles, `r fmt_num(v("ppc_rt_inside_pct_M4"), 1)`% fell inside the 95% predictive intervals, and observed median RTs were on average `r fmt_int(v("ppc_rt_median_bias_ms_M4"))` ms slower than predicted (@suppfig-ppc). The discrepancy was largest for minority responses ("different" on Standard trials, "same" on Easy trials and "different" on Hard trials), which were slower than predicted. After moment matching and exact refits, no observation in any compared model had a Pareto *k* above 0.7. Non-decision time changed with the RT cutoff: `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr015", "median"), 3)` s, `r fmt_num(v("t0_M4", "median"), 3)` s and `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr025", "median"), 3)` s at cutoffs of 0.15 s, 0.20 s and 0.25 s.

# 4 Discussion {.unnumbered}

We asked whether concurrent physical effort changes how older adults make perceptual decisions by reducing the quality of the evidence they accumulate, by changing how much evidence they require, or neither. High effort did not reduce evidence quality. Instead it shifted drift toward "same" on all trials. That shift appeared as an accuracy cost on Hard trials and, if anything, a small gain on Standard trials. Effort widened boundary separation by about 2%, an amount inside the region of practical equivalence, and left the starting point unchanged. `r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: one sentence on the pupil results.]")`

## 4.1 Drift criterion and evidence quality {.unnumbered}

A capacity account predicts that a concurrent grip draws on resources needed to evaluate the stimulus [@wickens2008]. That would reduce the separation between drift on identical and different trials. The effort × stimulus term, which measures that separation, was close to zero, and its interval allowed a small decline but not a large one. A capacity cost concentrated on the hardest trials would also make the effort effect depend on difficulty [@kahneman1973attention], but allowing it to do so did not improve prediction (`r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1", "se_delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1")`; @supptbl-model-comparison). The effort effect was a shift common to all trials. In diffusion-model terms, this is a change in the drift criterion: the reference point against which evidence is evaluated as favoring one response or the other [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. Because the upper boundary was "different," the criterion shift lowers drift on trials with a different probe, so those trials more often end in "same." On Standard trials the same shift moves drift further toward the correct response. The accuracy pattern follows from this. The Hard-trial cost is the change that a capacity account would predict, but here it arises from a change in the criterion rather than a loss of evidence quality. Accuracy alone cannot separate the two, because Hard trials were the trials on which the shift was most consequential.

The pattern is consistent with Chapter 1. Difficulty and effort did not interact in younger adults on any measure, which suggested that the two draw on separate resources at these effort levels. Chapter 2 reached the same conclusion from psychometric functions fitted to the same cohort's responses: high effort lowered "different" responses on identical and different trials alike, without making the psychometric function shallower. In the present older sample, effort likewise did not reduce evidence quality. This chapter has no younger comparison group, though, so it cannot show that the criterion shift is specific to older adults. The two chapters also differ in tasks and analyses.

The boundary results do not support either account of how effort changes caution. An adaptive-caution account predicts wider boundaries under high effort; a fatigue account predicts narrower ones. The estimated change was positive but practically negligible, and its interval included zero at the shortest RT cutoff. The data therefore show no meaningful change in caution under a 40% MVC grip. The starting point was also unchanged, so effort did not alter the prior preference for either response.

## 4.2 Effort and pupil size {.unnumbered}

`r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: the grip-period effort result, citing @zenon2014pupil.]")` `r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: the post-probe result and one sentence of interpretation, without arousal.]")` One interpretation of effort-related pupil changes comes from adaptive gain theory, which links pupil size to activity of the locus coeruleus–noradrenaline system [@astonjones2005; @joshi2016]. Isometric handgrip engages this system [@mather2020isometric], and the locus coeruleus is vulnerable in aging [@mather2016locus]. This study, however, neither manipulated nor measured locus coeruleus activity during the task, and pupil size also covaries with activity outside the locus coeruleus [@joshi2016].

## 4.3 Pupil size and boundary separation {.unnumbered}

`r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: Section 4.3.]")`

## 4.4 Limitations and future directions {.unnumbered}

**Boundary terms.** Boundary separation was allowed to vary with stimulus type, although stimulus types were intermixed and could not be anticipated. These terms let the model absorb RT differences between stimulus types that a diffusion model without across-trial variability cannot otherwise capture. This was most evident for minority responses, which were slower than predicted. That slow-error pattern is the signature of variability in drift across trials [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The effort contrasts were stable across model variants and RT cutoffs, but absolute parameter values depend on this choice. Models with across-trial variability in drift and non-decision time [@ratcliff2002estimating] would test whether the effort effects survive a better account of RT distributions.

**Response-signal design.** Because participants waited for a cue, non-decision time absorbed the enforced delay and changed almost one-for-one with the RT cutoff. It cannot be interpreted as encoding or motor time, and effort effects on it were not tested. The design also limits how much RT information constrains boundary separation. A free-response version of the task would test the boundary results more directly.

**Pupil sample and measure.** The pupil analyses used `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` of the `r v("n_final")` participants, selected on recording quality, and they are correlational at the level of trials. `r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: whether the effort effects in the pupil sample match the full sample.]")` The TEPR window included post-decision processing, and the grip-period measure combined effort-related dilation with trial-to-trial variation in the force produced. Entering the recorded trial-wise grip force as a covariate would separate the two.

**Design.** With two effort levels, the study cannot test non-monotonic effects of effort. Hard trials were answered incorrectly more often than correctly, so Hard-trial estimates reflect a strong bias toward "same" as well as low sensitivity. When participants with near-chance accuracy were excluded, the criterion shift kept its size, but its interval included zero. The effect is small and should be replicated.

**Response mapping.** "Different" was always given with the right index finger and "same" with the right middle finger, while the left hand held the grip. A bias acting on the evidence for one response therefore cannot be separated from the finger that gave that response; counterbalancing the mapping across participants would separate them.

**Physiological measures.** Pupil size was the only physiological measure. Because locus coeruleus activity was not measured during the task, links between the pupil results and the noradrenergic system remain interpretive.

## 4.5 Conclusion {.unnumbered}

In older adults, holding a 40% MVC grip during an auditory or visual same–different judgment shifted the drift criterion toward "same." It did not reduce the quality of the evidence accumulated or change response caution in a meaningful way. `r ch3_pending("[PENDING r12: the pupil sentence.]")`

## Analysis provenance (dissertation only) {.unnumbered}

Pupil samples were placed on a time axis at the recorded 250-Hz sampling rate, from 3 s before squeeze onset to the end of the confidence window. Earlier internal analyses that used a time axis derived from file timestamps were discarded, because that axis compressed time and misplaced the analysis windows; no result from those analyses is reported.

:::

```{r}
#| include: false
diag_dir <- params$diag_dir
if (is.null(diag_dir) || !nzchar(diag_dir)) {
  diag_dir <- "output/diagnostics/qmd_current"
}
dir.create(file.path(proj_root, diag_dir), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(
  data.frame(call_order = seq_along(.keys_used), key = .keys_used, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  file.path(proj_root, diag_dir, "keys_used.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```
